advisor.summary: The OpCo/PropCo split is the default architecture when a business and its building share one legal wrapper: operations run in one entity, the real estate (and sometimes heavy equipment) sits in another, and OpCo pays PropCo documented market rent under a real lease. The rent is an ordinary §162 deduction to OpCo, the rental stream escapes self-employment tax, and the structure delivers three things a single wrapper cannot: a liability wall between the judgment-exposed operating business and its most valuable asset, per-entity flexibility for PTET elections and §199A positioning, and independent exit paths — sell the business, keep the building as a rental to the buyer, or exchange the building under §1031 without touching operations. The tax friction is the self-rental recharacterization rule, whose income/loss asymmetry must be planned rather than discovered, and the timing rule is unforgiving: the structure is cheap to build at acquisition and expensive to retrofit out of an existing corporation. Advisory by design — the rent-flow math lives in the self-rental strategy; this record governs the structural design.
mechanics: The architecture: PropCo — typically an LLC taxed as a partnership or disregarded — owns the building; OpCo runs operations and pays rent under a written market-rate lease, deductible under §162(a)(3) as rent required for continued use of property OpCo does not own.

Liability isolation is the non-tax anchor: operating claims (injury, employment, contract) stop at OpCo, and property claims stop at PropCo — provided each entity maintains its own bank accounts, books, insurance, and formalities.

PropCo's rental income stays out of self-employment income under §1402(a)(1), but the self-rental rule of Reg. §1.469-2(f)(6) recharacterizes net rental income from a materially participating tenant business as nonpassive — while net losses stay passive — so the rent level decides which side of that asymmetry the client lands on.

The split does not cost the §199A position: rental to a commonly controlled trade or business is treated as a trade or business under Reg. §1.199A-1(b)(14), and Reg. §1.199A-4 aggregation can pool W-2 wages and UBIA across the pair when the limits bind.

The Reg. §1.469-4(d)(1) grouping election can treat the rental and the operating activity as one economic unit where ownership is proportionate — the standard answer when depreciation would otherwise strand self-rental losses.

State elections and exits unbundle: PTET elections run entity by entity, and PropCo can execute a §1031 exchange or outlive a business sale on its own — optionality that makes the split valuable long before any audit question arises.

authority.note: The rent deduction at OpCo — a genuine lease, at market rate, for property the payor does not own.
The self-rental recharacterization: net rental income from a materially participating tenant is nonpassive while losses stay passive — the asymmetry that drives rent-setting.
Real estate rentals sit outside self-employment income — the character benefit of the rent stream.
Self-rental to a commonly controlled trade or business is a §199A trade or business — the rent keeps its QBI character.
Aggregation rules that let commonly controlled entities share W-2 wages and UBIA for the §199A limits.
The grouping election treating the rental and operating business as one economic unit — the fix for trapped self-rental losses.
The like-kind exchange option preserved by holding the real property in its own entity.

requirements: A written market-rate lease between OpCo and PropCo — actually invoiced, paid, and enforced.
Genuine separateness: distinct bank accounts, books, insurance, and entity formalities — without them the liability wall collapses.
Clean title in PropCo, with lender consent, insurance re-titling, and any reassessment consequences resolved at transfer.
Proportionate ownership wherever §469 grouping or §199A aggregation is intended — both elections carry common-ownership conditions.
risks: The self-rental asymmetry is the recurring surprise: net rental income is nonpassive and cannot absorb the client's passive losses — a rule the courts have consistently upheld, most prominently in Krukowski v. Commissioner, 279 F.3d 547 (7th Cir. 2002) — while rent set low enough to produce losses leaves those losses passive and potentially trapped.
Non-market rent is the exam wedge: above-market rent invites reallocation and, with a C corporation tenant, constructive-dividend treatment; the comparable-lease file is the whole defense.
Retrofits are the expensive path — moving an appreciated building out of an existing corporation is a taxable event, so the analysis must precede the deed, not follow it.
Transfer frictions are real: lender due-on-sale and consent, insurance gaps during re-titling, and property tax reassessment in some jurisdictions.
The structure adds returns, leases, and bookkeeping; a client who will not keep up the formalities turns the liability wall into decoration.
stateNotes: Conformity: Missouri conforms to the federal passive-activity and rental characterizations through its federal starting point, so the recharacterization and grouping analysis flows straight into the state return.

PTET interaction: the split multiplies election flexibility — Missouri SALT Parity Act elections (RSMo §143.436) run entity by entity, so OpCo can elect while PropCo does not (or both can), letting the group route the deduction where it pays.

Missouri: retitling the building into PropCo triggers no Missouri real estate transfer tax — the state imposes none — removing a friction cost that complicates this structure elsewhere; lender consent and insurance re-titling still apply.
reviewChecklist: Market rent supported by a rent study or comparable leases kept in the file and refreshed at renewal.
Lease executed, invoices issuing, and payments actually moving between accounts.
Self-rental posture chosen deliberately — the asymmetry accepted, or the grouping election made with its disclosure statement.
§199A aggregation evaluated wherever the wage/UBIA limits bind.
Entity formalities verified annually: separate accounts, books, insurance, and minutes.
Any proposed retrofit from an existing corporation carries a written tax-cost analysis before anything moves.

client.teaser: Your business and your building do not belong in one legal basket — splitting them adds protection and options.
client.headline: Put your building and your business in separate boxes
plainEnglish: If your business owns its building, one lawsuit can threaten both. A claim against the business could reach the property, and a problem at the property could reach the business. Splitting them fixes that: operations in one company, real estate in another.

The business then pays fair-market rent to the property company, just as it would to any landlord. The rent is a normal deductible expense. And on your side, rent income avoids the extra payroll-style tax that business profits carry.

The split also keeps doors open. One day you might sell the business but keep the building and collect rent from the buyer. Or trade the building for a bigger one without touching the business. Separate boxes make both possible.
Special rules control how rent income and losses between your own companies get treated. We plan for those on day one, because the right choice depends on your whole picture.
client.analogy: It is like keeping savings and spending money in separate accounts — same owner, but trouble in one account cannot drain the other.
benefits: Shields your most valuable asset from business lawsuits and debts
Rent moves money to you free of payroll-style taxes
Freedom to sell, keep, or trade the building apart from the business
More levers for state tax elections and future planning
steps: WE design the structure — which assets go where, and who owns each company.
WE document a fair market rent and put a real lease in place.
YOU keep the companies separate: their own accounts, their own bills, rent paid on time.
WE review the rent, elections, and records each year so it all stays defensible.
clientCommitments: Pay the rent like a real tenant — on schedule, from the right account
Never mix the two companies' money or paperwork
Talk to us before refinancing, selling, or moving any property between companies

annualMaintenance: Review the rent against market each year with refreshed comparables
Check entity formalities: accounts, books, insurance, and lease renewal
Re-evaluate the grouping election and aggregation as facts change
Coordinate PTET elections across the entities each year
deliverables: Structure design memo covering asset placement, ownership, and elections
Written lease backed by a market-rent support file
Title, insurance, and lender transition checklist

suggest.reason: Separating operations from real estate improves liability walls and exit flexibility.

reviewTriggers: New self-rental or grouping-election case law
Client refinancing, acquisition, or exit events touching the real estate
